Inevitable crossover and the role of the soliton. —In primordial gas lacking molecular or metal coolants, radiative cooling is exponentially suppressed below  $ T \sim 10^4 $ K due to the Boltzmann factor associated with hydrogen collisional excitation (Lyman- $ \alpha $ cooling). Consequently, low-mass solitons ( $ M_s \lesssim 10^7 M_\odot $,  $ T_{\text{vir}} < 10^4 $ K) can maintain a stable, quasi-static atmosphere where the cooling time strictly exceeds the dynamical time ( $ t_{\text{cool}} > t_{\text{dyn}} $). However, as the soliton mass increases, the deeper potential well heats the gas above the  $ 10^4 $ K threshold, triggering highly efficient atomic cooling. In the high-temperature regime,  $ t_{\text{cool}} $ decreases more steeply with soliton mass (e.g.,  $ \propto M_s^{-3} $ for bremsstrahlung) than  $ t_{\text{dyn}} $ ( $ \propto M_s^{-2} $). This guarantees a crossover where  $ t_{\text{cool}} < t_{\text{dyn}} $. As illustrated in the updated Figure 2, this transition defines a critical mass scale at  $ M_{\text{crit}} \approx 2.8 \times 10^7 M_\odot $. The massive FDM cores relevant to LRDs ( $ M_s \gtrsim 10^8 M_\odot $) already reside deeply within this cooling-dominated region. In this unstable regime, the gas loses thermal support faster than the potential-defined dynamical time, triggering rapid inflow or collapse rather than maintaining a long-lived hot atmosphere. For comparison, at the same physical radius  $ r \sim r_c $, a BH-only (“naked”) potential has  $ M_{\text{enc}} \approx M_{\text{BH}} $ and therefore a longer dynamical time than the soliton case (because  $ M_{\text{enc,sol}} \geq M_{\text{BH}} $). Thus, if  $ t_{\text{cool}} \lesssim t_{\text{dyn}} $ holds in the soliton container, it holds a fortiori in the BH-only limit. The role of the soliton is therefore not to stabilize the gas, but to define the characteristic  $ \sim 50-100 $ pc scale relevant to LRDs and to motivate considering a quasi-spherical, volume-filling atmosphere at that scale.

The primary observational puzzle of LRDs is their X-ray faintness. Using the conservative estimate in Eq. (3), typical columns can reach  $ N_{\mathrm{H}} \sim 10^{24}-10^{25} \, \mathrm{cm}^{-2} $. The Thomson optical depth is  $ \tau_T = \sigma_T N_{\mathrm{H}} \simeq 0.67 \, (N_{\mathrm{H}} / 10^{24} \, \mathrm{cm}^{-2}) $. For  $ \tau_T \gtrsim 1 $, the direct soft X-ray continuum is strongly suppressed. We expect the observed X-ray signal to be dominated by a scattered fraction  $ f_{\mathrm{scat}} $. For typical AGN geometries,  $ f_{\mathrm{scat}} \sim 1 - 5\% $, implying a suppression of the apparent  $ L_X $ by  $ \sim 1.5 - 2 $ dex, consistent with Maiolino et al. (2024).
#### 3.2. Dust Attenuation and Broad Line Visibility

Recent analyses suggest that LRDs are best described as young SMBHs embedded in compact, physically thick obscurers (“dense ionized cocoons” and/or heavy dust shrouds) with column densities  $ N_{\mathrm{H}} \gtrsim 10^{24} \, \mathrm{cm}^{-2} $ (e.g., Rusakov et al. 2026). Our FDM soliton framework provides a natural origin for such a geometry: unlike a rotationally supported thin disk, the soliton produces a quasi-spherical potential well on the characteristic scale  $ r_c \sim 50-100 \, \mathrm{pc} $, so gas inflowing into the core can initially fill a large fraction of the volume.
A simple parameterized cocoon geometry.—We parameterize the obscurer as extending from an inner dust sublimation scale  $ r_{in} $ to an observable effective radius

with a line-of-sight covering factor  $ f_{\mathrm{cov}} \gtrsim 0.5 $. A convenient phenomenological description is a biconical polar opening with half-opening angle  $ \theta $, for which  $ f_{\mathrm{cov}} \simeq \cos \theta $. In this picture, broad lines remain visible either through low-column sightlines (gaps) or via scattering into the line of sight, while the high covering factor naturally accounts for the high detection rate of obscured LRDs (e.g., Greene et al. 2024).

Granularity and clumpiness in the soliton core.—A specific ingredient of the FDM core is its intrinsic time-dependent granularity arising from wave interference. Order-unity density fluctuations (“granules”;  $ \delta\rho/\rho \sim 1 $) produce persistent gravitational stirring on timescales comparable to the soliton dynamical/oscillation time. These perturbations can promote and help maintain a clumpy cocoon/torus morphology, providing a complementary route to clumpiness beyond magnetic or radiation-driven instabilities.
